blocks.text: A GPU, graphics processing unit, is specialized hardware built around massive parallelism, thousands of relatively simple cores working simultaneously, a design that happens to fit the matrix heavy computation deep learning relies on extremely well.
This topic covers the basics of what makes a GPU suited to fine-tuning, setting up the more specific memory and precision topics covered throughout the rest of this Training Infrastructure module.
1. Why GPUs Fit Deep Learning So Well

blocks.alt: Why GPUs Fit Deep Learning So Well
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101452-20641279.png

Deep learning computation, especially the matrix multiplications at the heart of the attention mechanism and feed-forward layers covered in the Foundation Models module, consists of an enormous number of small, independent arithmetic operations that can all run at the same time, exactly what a GPU large number of parallel cores is built to handle efficiently.
2. GPU vs CPU, The Core Architectural Difference

blocks.alt: GPU vs CPU, The Core Architectural Difference
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101452-293239278.png

A CPU is built around a small number of very capable cores, optimized for handling varied, sequential tasks quickly, while a GPU trades that per core sophistication for sheer quantity, thousands of simpler cores that excel specifically at doing the same kind of operation across a huge amount of data simultaneously.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Hardware","Core Count","Best Suited For"],"rows":[["CPU","Few, powerful, general purpose","Varied, sequential tasks"],["GPU","Many, simpler, specialized","Massively parallel, repetitive computation"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Cores, Memory, and Bandwidth
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101452-384072443.png

A GPU capability is shaped by more than just core count, its memory bandwidth, how quickly data can move between memory and the cores actually doing computation, matters just as much, since even a very powerful set of cores sits idle if data cannot be fed to them fast enough.
4. What a Forward and Backward Pass Actually Uses a GPU For

blocks.alt: What a Forward and Backward Pass Actually Uses a GPU For
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101453-925626370.png

Both the forward pass, computing predictions, and the backward pass, computing gradients, covered in the earlier Causal Language Modeling Loss topic, consist overwhelmingly of matrix multiplications and related operations, exactly the kind of workload a GPU parallel architecture accelerates dramatically compared to a CPU.

code.content:
# A conceptual illustration, matrix multiplication is the core GPU workload
output = input_matrix @ weight_matrix
# GPUs parallelize this operation across thousands of cores at once

blocks.text: 5. GPU Memory as the Practical Constraint

blocks.alt: GPU Memory as the Practical Constraint
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101453-686985747.png

In practice, the single most common constraint fine-tuning projects run into is not raw compute speed but available GPU memory, VRAM, covered in depth in the next topic of this module, since a model and everything needed to train it must actually fit before training can begin at all.
6. Common GPU Tiers for Fine-Tuning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101661-849624944.png

Fine-tuning happens across a wide range of hardware tiers, from consumer GPUs originally built for gaming, offering modest VRAM but wide accessibility, up to specialized data center GPUs with far more memory and compute, built specifically for large scale machine learning workloads, each tier suited to a different scale of fine-tuning project.
7. Utilization, Are You Actually Using the GPU Well

blocks.alt: Utilization, Are You Actually Using the GPU Well
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101663-209387.png

Owning a powerful GPU does not guarantee a training run actually uses it efficiently, low utilization, where the GPU sits partially idle waiting for data or coordination overhead, wastes available compute potential, a consideration that becomes especially relevant once distributed training, covered later in this module, enters the picture.

blocks.title: This connects to the batch size discussion in Training Fundamentals
blocks.content: A mini-batch size too small to keep a GPU cores fully busy is one common, straightforward cause of poor utilization, worth checking before assuming a more exotic infrastructure problem is at fault.

blocks.text: 8. GPUs vs Other Accelerators

While GPUs remain the most widely used hardware for fine-tuning covered throughout this course, other specialized accelerators exist, each with their own tradeoffs in cost, availability, and framework support, though GPUs benefit from by far the broadest tooling and community support across the fine-tuning ecosystem today.
9. Choosing a GPU for a Fine-Tuning Project

Choosing an appropriate GPU comes down primarily to how much VRAM a specific model and training configuration actually needs, a calculation this module builds toward across its remaining topics, rather than raw compute speed alone, since a training run that does not fit in memory cannot run regardless of how fast the underlying cores are.
Worked Example

A developer choosing between two available GPUs, one with more raw compute cores but less memory, and one with somewhat fewer cores but significantly more VRAM, picks the higher memory option for their fine-tuning project, since their specific model and batch size configuration would not fit in the lower memory GPU at all, making its extra compute speed irrelevant.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing a GPU based on raw compute speed alone without checking whether the model actually fits in its available memory
Assuming a powerful GPU automatically means high utilization, without checking whether batch size or data loading are limiting factors
Confusing consumer and data center GPU tiers without considering which one actually matches the project scale
Overlooking memory bandwidth as a factor separate from core count when evaluating GPU capability

blocks.text: Practice

For a GPU you have access to or are considering, look up its available VRAM, and compare that figure against the rough memory needs of a fine-tuning project you have in mind, confirming for yourself whether that specific GPU could realistically support it.
Key Takeaway

GPUs accelerate deep learning through massive parallelism across thousands of simpler cores, well matched to the matrix heavy computation of both the forward and backward pass, and while raw compute speed matters, available GPU memory is typically the more immediate practical constraint that determines whether a given fine-tuning project can run on a specific piece of hardware at all.
